quests.passageTopic: Incident Review: Online Ordering Outage, 12 March
quests.passage: Summary. On 12 March, customers were unable to place orders for 3 hours and 40 minutes, beginning at 6:05 p.m., the busiest period of the week. Roughly 4,100 orders were lost or delayed. Timeline. At 5:50 p.m., an engineer deployed a routine update to the discount-code system. At 6:05 p.m., the order page began returning errors; the monitoring system generated an alert, but it was sent to a mailbox that is checked only during office hours. The first sign that anything was wrong came at 6:32 p.m., when a customer-service agent noticed a surge of complaint calls and escalated it by telephone. Engineers identified the update as the likely cause at 7:10 p.m. but initially hesitated to reverse it, because a reversal would also remove a security fix that had been included in the same release. After a discussion between the engineering and security teams, the update was reversed at 9:25 p.m., and the security fix was reapplied separately by 9:45 p.m. Contributing factors. The update was released at a time of peak demand, which the deployment guidelines discourage but do not prohibit. The alert system worked as designed, but the destination was not appropriate for an urgent warning. Two unrelated changes had been bundled into one release, which complicated the decision to reverse it. Actions. Alerts will be routed to the on-call engineer's phone. Releases will be prohibited between 5:00 and 9:00 p.m. on weekdays. Security fixes will be released separately from other changes.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Two Views on Short-Term Rentals
quests.passage: Councillor Dara Voss (supporting a ban on whole-home rentals under 30 days): "In our old town, one in six homes is now a holiday rental. Families who grew up here cannot find homes, because landlords make more renting by the night than by the year. Schools in the old town have lost a third of their pupils in a decade, and last year the council received more than 300 complaints about noise and rubbish from residents living beside holiday lets. Hosts say they depend on this income, and I believe them, but the community cannot be run as an extension of the tourism industry. A ban would return around 900 homes to the long-term market." Mr. Ibrahim Sayed (opposing the ban): "The ban would be a blunt tool. Most hosts are not investors; they are residents renting a spare room or their own home while they travel. A ban on whole-home rentals would catch them too. Meanwhile, the real driver of high rents is the shortage of new housing, which this council has failed to address for twenty years. Banning rentals would cost the local economy an estimated $14 million a year in visitor spending, and there is no guarantee that landlords would rent to locals instead of leaving homes empty or selling to second-home buyers."

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Sunday Dinner
quests.passage: Naomi had rehearsed three topics of conversation in the car, and so far she had used none of them. Luka's mother passed the potatoes with the air of someone handing over evidence. "Luka tells me you changed jobs again," she said. "He tells me you're an adviser now. For whom?" "A small firm," said Naomi. "We help schools plan their budgets." "Schools," repeated Mrs. Varga. "Well. That's steady." Across the table, Luka's father cleared his throat and asked whether anyone had seen the match on Saturday. Nobody had. He seemed relieved to have been refused. The potatoes, Naomi noticed, had gone cold. "Luka says you grew up near the coast," Mrs. Varga continued. "Is your family there still?" "My mother is," said Naomi. "She'd like to meet you both, sometime." It was the first sentence she had planned, and she had not expected it to land the way it did. Mrs. Varga's fork paused. Then she smiled, a real one, small and a little surprised. "I would like that," she said, "very much." Luka, who had been studying his plate as if it contained instructions, looked up for the first time in ten minutes. Neither woman mentioned jobs again for the rest of the meal; the conversation moved, tentatively, to coastlines, ferries and the best way to cook fish.

quests.passageTopic: Travel Insurance Claim Conditions: Cancellation Cover
quests.passage: Cancellation cover reimburses non-refundable trip costs if you must cancel for a covered reason. Covered reasons are: serious illness or injury of the insured person or a close relative, death of a close relative, jury service, redundancy of the insured person where they have been employed continuously for at least two years, and damage to the insured person's home making it uninhabitable. Voluntary changes of plan, fear of travelling, and cancellation because of a pre-existing medical condition are not covered unless the condition was declared and accepted by the insurer when the policy was purchased. You must notify the insurer within 48 hours of the event that forces you to cancel, and you must tell the travel provider immediately, since claims will be reduced if costs increase through delay. A medical certificate is required for any illness-related claim. Claims for trips booked through a travel agent must also include the agent's written confirmation of the booking date. The maximum payment is $4,000 per person, and the first $150 of every claim is deducted as an excess. Close relative means a spouse, parent, child, brother or sister, grandparent or grandchild. If the policy was purchased more than 14 days after the trip was booked, cover for cancellation due to illness begins only after a seven-day waiting period.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Restaurant Review: The Second Visit
quests.passage: When I first reviewed Brasa in 2021, I called it the most exciting opening of the year. The chef, Ana Duarte, cooked over open fire with a confidence that made even the vegetables memorable, and I left wanting to return the next night. So it is with some reluctance that I report a very different experience this spring. Duarte left in January, and her successor, the capable but cautious Tomas Weil, has kept the menu while quietly sanding down its edges. The famous charred cabbage now arrives pale and polite. A lamb dish, once seasoned so boldly that it started conversations, tasted of very little beyond itself. Nothing was wrong, exactly, and that is the problem: the kitchen now cooks as though it were afraid of complaints. Service remains excellent, and the room is as warm as ever. The wine list, at least, remains as interesting and fairly priced as before. I do not doubt that Weil is talented, and some of his own additions, a tart of leeks and sheep's cheese in particular, hinted at what he could do if allowed to stop imitating. But a restaurant that was once an argument has become a reassurance. For the prices charged, I expect more than reassurance. I will return in the autumn, in the hope that Weil has found his own voice.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Pricing Decision at Page & Co.
quests.passage: Page & Co., an independent bookstore, sells new paperbacks at the publisher's recommended price. Faced with competition from an online retailer, the owner, Helen Brandt, considered a 15 percent discount on all paperbacks. Her accountant estimated that the store's average margin on paperbacks was 40 percent before the discount. The discount would therefore reduce the margin on each book to 25 percent of the original price, a drop of more than a third in profit per book. To break even on total profit, she calculated, sales would need to rise by 60 percent. A survey of 200 customers suggested that the discount might raise purchases by about a quarter, far short of what was needed. Her accountant also reminded her that rent and wages would not fall. However, the survey also revealed that customers valued things the online retailer could not offer: staff recommendations, a children's reading corner, and the ability to hold a book before buying. Instead of discounting, Brandt decided to invest in these features, adding two evening events a month and a small subscription service in which staff choose a book for members. The online retailer's prices remained lower throughout. After a year, paperback sales were unchanged but subscription income had added the equivalent of 9 percent to annual profit, and she had not touched her prices.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: The Penny Post
quests.passage: Before 1840, sending a letter in Britain was expensive and strange. The recipient, not the sender, paid, and the cost depended on distance and the number of sheets. A letter from London to Edinburgh could cost a laborer a day's wages. Unsurprisingly, people found ways around the system: families agreed on codes written on the outside of the envelope, which the recipient could read and refuse to accept, thereby receiving the news for free. Rowland Hill, a schoolteacher turned reformer, argued in 1837 that the high prices were self-defeating. He observed that the actual cost of carrying a letter was a tiny fraction of the charge, and that the expensive bureaucracy of calculating and collecting fees consumed most of the difference. His proposal was radical: a uniform rate of one penny for any letter under a certain weight, paid in advance by the sender with an adhesive stamp. The Post Office resisted, and some officials predicted financial disaster. When the scheme began in 1840, however, the volume of letters rose from about 76 million a year to more than 160 million within two years. Revenue initially fell but recovered within a decade as the volume grew. Hill's reform shows that a price which seems generous can sometimes produce more, not less, for the one who sets it.

quests.passage: Letter from customer: "I bought a laptop from your store on 3 February. On 19 July the screen began flickering, and by August it would not turn on. The laptop is covered by a two-year manufacturer's warranty, but when I called your service department I was told that it could not be repaired under warranty because it had been 'subjected to liquid damage.' I have never spilled anything on it. I would like a replacement or a refund." Reply from the company: "Thank you for your letter. Our technician has examined your laptop and found corrosion on the main board consistent with liquid exposure. Such damage is excluded from the manufacturer's warranty. We appreciate that you do not recall any spillage, and we are not suggesting you have been dishonest; high humidity or a small amount of condensation can sometimes produce similar corrosion. However, the exclusion applies regardless of how the exposure occurred. As a gesture of goodwill, we can offer to repair the laptop at cost, which we estimate at $210, a saving of about 40 percent on our usual charge. Alternatively, you may wish to ask your home insurer whether the damage would be covered. We value your custom and hope to resolve this to your satisfaction. Please let us know your preference within 14 days."
